title: Second Pick Wins
pitch: Choose a three-flip coin pattern; a smug bot picks its own after seeing yours, and a flip-by-flip race decides who sees their pattern first. The visitor loses far more than half the time, for any pattern they try, then cranks the race to ten million flips and watches the bot's edge settle on exact fractions like 2 to 1, and finally flips the table by taking the second pick themselves. A red-and-black card mode with tricks turns the cascade of flips into a visible deck.
whyNow: Timeless. The result is a clean argument-loser: the game is fair in each pick yet rigged by order of choice, and nothing like it has shipped.

research.summary: In Penney's game two players each pick a short heads-tails pattern and the one that appears first in a fair coin sequence wins. Because picking is sequential, the second picker can always choose a reply that beats the first pick; for every three-flip pattern a better reply exists. A short rule builds the reply, and Conway's leading-number method gives exact odds. A card version (red/black cards, collecting tricks) exists. The page can show the full payoff matrix of lengths 3 to 5, the exact Markov-chain odds next to a ten-million-flip seeded Monte Carlo, and expected waiting times, where the winning pattern is not always the quicker one on average, which is what makes the loss feel unfair.

facts.claim: In Penney's game the second chooser has an advantage: for any pattern of three flips there is another three-flip pattern strictly more likely to appear first.
Conway's leading-number algorithm gives the odds between two patterns; a no-arbitrage proof was published in 2019.
Reply rule: against a first pick, flip the second symbol, put it in front, and drop the last symbol; HTH is answered by HHT.
A card variant with red and black cards (Humble-Nishiyama) uses the same logic, with tricks collected instead of single wins.
Reported by one write-up: HHT precedes HTH about two thirds of the time; the page computes this exactly itself.

design.coreLoop: Pick a pattern (length 3, later 4 or 5); the bot answers; run one live race flip by flip with a bar-chart tension, then batches of 1,000 or 10 million; track the running win rate converging to the exact fraction. Modes: you pick first (you lose), the bot picks first (you find the reply and win), and a puzzle mode where you must find the pattern with the best guaranteed odds. Replay value comes from lengths 4 and 5, the card-deck mode where depletion changes the odds, and a streak of 'argument' challenges.
sophisticationHooks: Exact odds via Markov-chain absorption (Conway leading numbers cross-checked), versus seeded worker Monte Carlo with error bars
Payoff matrix heatmap for all patterns of length 3 to 5 with the best-reply path highlighted, plus a cycle view showing the non-transitive loop
Expected waiting time panel showing the pattern that arrives later on average still wins the race
Red/black deck mode played without replacement with tricks, so the visitor sees the effect survive in a real deck; hash state with seed and picks
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: pattern picker, bot reply engine, race animation, exact solver, worker Monte Carlo, payoff matrix, waiting-time panel, card mode, about panel, hash state. Cut: lengths above 5, multiplayer, sound.
risks: The 2 to 3 odds numbers beyond the sources are computed by the page and labelled 'computed here'
The ten-million-flip race must stay responsive: chunked in a worker with a progress bar
Card-mode odds differ from coin odds; both computed exactly by enumeration or DP and shown separately, never mixed
Plain Penney content is common online; the matrix, deck mode and waiting-time angle give it a distinct feel
